verdict: The two pages measure almost the same: body text starts at 622 px and wraps at about 2245 px on both, both are near-white, and both have generous side margins. That leaves the left edge as the deciding difference. A lets its heading markers push the headings out of line with the body, so the column wobbles at every section break. B hangs the markers in the gutter, and its left edge runs straight from top to bottom. A's extra 2 px of leading and slightly brighter paper don't make up for that.

states.name: narrow
states.gap: B's text block runs lower down the page. The paragraph ends at y≈862 and the next '## What the sea keeps' heading is cut off at the bottom edge (y≈970–1000), so there is no clean bottom margin and the frame feels cropped. A still has about 47 px of paper below its last line.
states.gapTheirs: A's body text is set looser: each character takes about 24.6 px across (57 characters over 233→1637 px) against B's 23.8 px (60 characters over 236→1666). So A's first line breaks after 'boat.' where B fits 'It'. The whole passage wraps one word earlier per line, and the page reads as spaced-out typewriter type rather than an even grey block.
states.verdict: Both use the same #F7F7F7 paper, the same ~63–64 px line spacing and nearly the same ~1450 px text width, so the fight is over texture and framing. A's wider character spacing and heavier strokes turn the paragraph into a coarse typewriter texture, and its rounded window corners with a blue-grey edge pull the eye off the page. B's tighter, lighter setting gives a steadier grey block that is easier to read for an hour, even though it lets the next heading fall off the bottom of the window. I'd write in B, but not by much.

states.name: short
states.gap: The measure is a little tighter and the lines sit a little closer. Glyph advance is ≈26.8 vs 26.4 device px per character (1134 vs 1118 display px over the same 61-character line), so a paragraph line wraps one word sooner ('empty,' / 'and'). Line pitch is ≈74 vs 76 device px, which makes the paragraphs look slightly more packed.
states.gapTheirs: The heading marker isn't hung in the margin. '# ' starts at x≈622 device px, on the same edge as the body text, so the heading words start about 51 px to the right of the body's left edge (≈673 vs 622). The text column's left edge breaks at every heading, and the left margin reads as 622 px for the body but 673 px for heading words.
states.verdict: Both pages use the same near-white paper and a centred column of about 1630 px with roughly 625 px of margin on each side. The real difference is the left edge. B hangs the '#' out in the margin, so heading and body share one straight edge at x=622. A pushes the heading words in by a marker's width, so the column's left edge jogs at every heading, and you notice it every time your eye goes back to the start of a line. B pays for that with slightly tighter lines and a wider advance that wraps a word early, but a crooked left edge is harder to ignore than 2 px of leading.
